messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 79

# The Weight of Hands

Maya is a 35-year-old Filipino physical therapist who has been married for three years to her current husband, a man she describes as "the gentlest person I've ever known." She says this with a kind of wonder, as if she still cannot fully believe it. Before him, there was Daniel — four years of a relationship that began with tenderness and ended with her standing in a hospital parking lot at two in the morning, pressing a bag of ice against her jaw, trying to decide whether to go inside.

She never went inside. She drove herself home instead.

The abuse began gradually, the way she now explains nerve damage to her patients — imperceptibly at first, then suddenly undeniable. By the third year with Daniel, the violence had become a rhythm she organized her life around. She learned to read the particular silence that preceded his rages, the way his shoulders would draw inward before his hands moved outward. She became, she says, an expert in him. She knew exactly which muscles were tensing before the strike came.

The final incident happened on a Tuesday evening. Daniel slammed her head against the edge of the kitchen counter, and she lost consciousness briefly. When she came to, she was on the tile floor, and he was sitting at the kitchen table, eating dinner. She left that night with her car keys and her work bag. She did not go back.

That was four years ago. By any external measure, Maya has rebuilt her life completely. She has a career she loves, a husband who treats her with consistent care, and a small home with a garden she tends on weekends. But the past is not finished with her.

She wakes most nights between two and three in the morning, heart pounding, convinced that someone is in the room. She lies rigid beside her sleeping husband, listening, cataloguing sounds — the refrigerator hum, traffic outside, the house settling — until her body slowly releases its emergency. Some mornings she arrives at the clinic already exhausted, moving through her patient caseload on discipline alone.

The hardest part of her work, she admits, is her hands. Physical therapy requires constant touch, and she is good at it — her patients trust her, and she is skilled at reading bodies in pain. But there are moments, particularly when a male patient flinches or moves unexpectedly, when something seizes in her chest and her hands go briefly still. She recovers quickly enough that no one notices. She has become skilled at that too.

She cannot tolerate raised voices. In the break room recently, two colleagues had a loud, laughing argument about a sports game, and Maya found herself in the supply closet, back against the shelving, waiting for her breathing to slow. She told no one. She returned to her patient and finished the session.

At home, she monitors her husband's moods with an attention she recognizes as disproportionate and cannot stop. When he is quiet, she scans his face for signs she knows intellectually are not there. She has begun avoiding the kitchen in the evenings. She cannot fully explain this to herself. She knows the tile floor in her current kitchen is different. She knows everything is different. Her body does not seem to know this.

She describes a persistent sense of being somehow outside her own life — watching herself move through it, competent and composed, while something essential remains back on that kitchen floor, waiting. She has not told her husband the full extent of what happened with Daniel. She has not told her mother. She has not told anyone, she says, until now.

She sits with her hands folded in her lap — the same hands that help other people heal — and says she is tired of being so careful all the time. She says she would like to feel safe inside her own body. She says this quietly, as though it is almost too much to ask.
